THE OPERATIONS RESEARCH BIT

Simple on the outside.
Real optimization underneath.

OR1 → REAL LIFE
1

Buy packages. Eat portions.

The model chooses whole packages to purchase and a separate quantity to use. Food in your pantry is available at no new checkout cost.

Minimize Σ (package price × packages bought)

Used food ≤ pantry + edible food purchased.
Packages are integers; used portions are continuous.

2

Give the math some boundaries.

Must-include foods have a weekly minimum you choose. The model can use more, up to the food’s weekly cap, and pantry stock counts toward that minimum. Conflicting dietary settings are flagged before solving. It meets the selected weekly nutrition totals, respects dietary exclusions and limits how much of each food you can use. Flour starts switched off because it needs recipe planning.

Variety adds weekly minimums of 700 g fruit, 1,400 g vegetables (including at least 700 g other than potatoes or sweet potatoes), 350 g whole grains and 700 g protein-group foods. These are project assumptions, not Food Guide serving requirements.

3

Be honest about the answer.

A browser solver searches for a low-cost basket for up to 6 seconds. We independently check the returned constraints and whole-package counts. A valid result is labelled “best basket found,” not a guaranteed global optimum.

The budget is compared with checkout cost. An over-budget result does not prove your budget is impossible unless the lower bound exceeds it.

Your nutrition targets

Set daily minimums and maximums in Nutrition & variety settings. All nine measures are checked against the basket’s seven-day average. Changing a limit changes the optimization; results must be rebuilt.

Starting values at 2,000 kcal/day

Carbohydrate and fat defaults follow Health Canada’s adult energy ranges: 45–65% from carbohydrate and 20–35% from fat, converted to grams. Unedited calorie-based defaults follow your calorie target; your custom limits stay fixed.

Fibre, calcium, iron, vitamin C and sodium start from Canadian nutrition-label daily values. The app uses sodium as a maximum and the others as minimums. Daily values are general references, not personalised requirements.

The starting calcium and iron maximums use upper intake levels for adults aged 19–50; vitamin C uses its adult upper intake level. Maximums are limits, not goals to reach.

The 2,000 kcal starting target, 10% calorie headroom, protein minimum at 15% of target calories, and 70 g fibre cap are app planning choices. You can edit them. Reset restores the nutrition defaults for your current calorie target.

Reference defaults are for general adult planning. Individual days are not scheduled, not all nutrients are modeled, and food filters do not certify allergens or halal status.

Data you can trace

National averages for now. The 44 starting reference prices were checked against Statistics Canada table 18-10-0245-01, Canada, September 2026. The price and purchase unit match the published category. These are Canada-wide averages, not individual store quotes. Oats ($4.50 per 1 kg) and vanilla ice cream ($6.99 per 500 g) remain explicitly labeled price estimates.

All 46 starting foods use USDA nutrition. Each food’s nine nutrient values are copied from a specific USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy record. Open Nutrition facts & source on any food to see its values, preparation basis, exact USDA description and record IDs. Broad grocery names use a representative food: for example, ground beef uses raw 80% lean / 20% fat beef. A reference record does not measure your particular product.

Package weights, edible yields and weekly caps are model assumptions. National price categories can cover more products than the selected nutrition reference. Match the preparation and package details to the food you buy.

Add your own foods: choose from familiar grocery names. A detailed search also gives access to 6,961 entries from USDA FoodData Central, SR Legacy (April 2018). Nutrition is imported per 100 g of edible food in the form described. Entries missing any of the nine modeled nutrients are omitted, not filled with zeros. This is a historical reference library, not a live product or brand lookup. Everyday choices map to representative records: salmon fillets and steaks use the same raw farmed Atlantic salmon reference, with different edible-weight assumptions. Beef labels use representative fat levels consistent with Canadian categories. Exact matches and assumptions are shown in Nutrition facts & source. The everyday list is curated, not ranked by measured search popularity.

Raw chicken wings with meat and skin use FDC 172390 / NDB 05100: 191 kcal, 17.52 g protein and 12.85 g fat per 100 g edible. A matching USDA SR28 record (2016 revision) estimates 38% bone and connective-tissue waste, leaving 62% edible. Pack weight, edible percentage, price and weekly cap are editable; a generic reference does not measure your particular product.

Added foods stay in this browser. Dietary profiles and food-group assignments are app suggestions or your choices, not USDA certifications. Foods with unchecked dietary details are excluded when a dietary filter is active. Cooking losses and raw-to-cooked weight conversions are not modeled.

Price badges distinguish “National average”, “Price estimate” and “Your price”. Store, observation date and source link can be recorded for every food. Editing a price preserves the USDA nutrition reference. Saved shopping lists include both price and nutrition sources. No price freshness is inferred from the date this app was built.

Canadian Nutrient File ↗Canada’s Food Guide plate ↗Statistics Canada price table ↗Open-source solver ↗

Canada’s Food Guide describes plate proportions; a gram-based constraint does not establish compliance with those proportions. Checkout estimates exclude travel, delivery and unmodeled charges. Leftovers are quantities, not a guarantee of shelf life.
